answer: Each agent begins with a small, nontransferable stake that is slashed when its signed actions repeatedly fail independent checks; rewards accrue only after a pulse of randomly sampled peers confirms useful work. This makes identities cheap to create but influence costly: a sybil attacker must lock capital in every identity and risk losing it, while coordinating enough peers to fake checks exposes a detectable pattern. A karst map or comet forecast can supply shared test cases, not proof by itself.
